claim: Single-pass review is a linear pipeline (diff ingestion, model evaluation against rules, comment generation) while agentic review shifts from a tool that posts comments to an agent that takes actions.
quote: The next generation of AI code review tools won't stop at flagging a missing test: they'll write it, open a follow-up pull request, and run it through CI.

claim: Qodo's agentic review uses a Context Engine indexing four layers (rules, codebase, PR history, business requirements) and deploys 15+ specialized agentic workflows rather than a monolithic reviewer.
quote: Purpose-built for agentic code review, Qodo's context engine pulls context from across various context sources to provide a continuous, multi-dimensional understanding of complex coding environments.

claim: Greptile's agentic architecture builds a code graph of files, functions and dependencies and runs parallel agents that assess impact beyond the diff with full codebase context.
quote: Parallel agents review changes and assess their impact beyond the diff.

claim: Agentic workflows receive a high-level goal, decompose it, and run an Observe-Think-Act loop where step N depends on prior results, unlike single-pass prompting; a verification gap arises when the same model plans, acts and evaluates, mitigated by separate critic models.
quote: the model's behavior at step N depends on what happened at steps 1 through N-1.

claim: In 2026 CodeRabbit is the cheapest dedicated per-seat tool ($24/dev/mo) running 40+ linters plus LLM reasoning for PR summaries and inline fixes; Greptile ($30/dev/mo, 50-review cap +$1 overage) indexes the whole codebase into a dependency graph for cross-file context; Cursor BugBot and Graphite are priciest at $40/seat; CodeRabbit and Qodo cover GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/Azure DevOps while BugBot and Greptile cover GitHub/GitLab only.
quote: CodeRabbit is the cheapest per-seat dedicated tool at $24/dev/month, while Greptile mixes the two ($30/dev/month with a 50-review cap and $1 overage). Bugbot and Graphite are the most expensive per-seat options at $40.

claim: On a 118-bug benchmark Macroscope detected 48% of production bugs at 98% precision and ~2.55 comments/PR (usage-based ~$0.95/review), ranking ahead of CodeRabbit (46%), Cursor BugBot (42%) and Greptile (24%).
quote: Macroscope is the best AI code review tool for GitHub in 2026. It detected 48% of production bugs — the highest of any tool tested — while maintaining 98% precision and averaging just 2.55 comments per PR. Macroscope's usage-based pricing ($0.05/KB, averaging $0.95/review)

claim: Graphite is a stacked-PR/merge-queue/CI platform whose Diamond AI reviewer drew mixed feedback (few false positives but missed most critical bugs); Graphite was acquired by Cursor in December 2025 to merge Diamond with BugBot.
quote: One user summarized feedback on Graphite's Diamond reviewer as "pretty useless" because it gave very few false positives but also missed most critical bugs. In December 2025, Graphite was acquired by Cursor.

claim: GitHub Copilot code review shares a capped pool of 'premium requests' with all other Copilot AI features (no unlimited plan); its March 2026 agentic architecture upgrade moved review quality from 'barely useful' to 'meaningfully helpful'.
quote: code review shares a capped pool of "premium requests" with all other Copilot AI features — there's no unlimited plan. The March 2026 agentic architecture was a genuine improvement that moved it from "barely useful" to "meaningfully helpful."

claim: Ellipsis focuses on automated review and PR summarization with whole-PR agents that can write tests or refactor (users report ~13% faster merges); Sourcery began as a Python code-quality tool, expanded to JS/TS and Go, and leads on pattern-based refactoring rather than pure bug detection.
quote: Ellipsis focuses on two things: automated code review and PR summarization... users reporting that Ellipsis helps "merge code 13% faster"... Sourcery started as a Python-specific code quality tool and has expanded to JavaScript/TypeScript and Go, with its strength being pattern-based refactoring

claim: Korbit AI offers Korbit AI Mentor, a PR code-review assistant emphasizing mentorship/education that flags critical bugs, performance issues and security vulnerabilities while giving contextual advice.
quote: Korbit.ai offers Korbit AI Mentor, a code-review assistant that emphasizes mentorship and education and securely reviews your code in pull requests, focusing on critical bugs, performance issues, and security vulnerabilities.

claim: Baz Reviewer runs code changes through multiple aspect-specific review flows (idiomatic usage, conciseness, test quality, conventions), enriching the diff with context, and runs inside GitHub suggesting without blocking.
quote: Baz runs code through multiple review flows, each focusing on a specific aspect of programming—whether it's idiomatic usage for the language, code conciseness, test quality, or adherence to best practices and organizations' conventions.

claim: Baz offers Custom Reviewers trained on a team's own PR history plus a Prompt Playground, and a Spec Review Agent that renders implementations in a live Preview Environment to validate UI against Figma designs and behavior against Jira specs.
quote: Baz offers Custom Reviewers powered by your team's own pull request history, paired with the Prompt Playground, letting you encode, test, and evolve your team's engineering brain into a system of principles that AI can use.

claim: Anthropic launched Claude Code Review on March 9, 2026 as a multi-agent GitHub PR reviewer (parallel agents for logic bugs, security, regressions, plus an aggregator), billed on token usage averaging ~$15-25/review, available as a beta research preview for Team and Enterprise plans.
quote: Claude Code Review is an automated code review tool launched on March 9, 2026, by Anthropic... When a pull request opens on GitHub, Claude Code Review deploys a team of AI agents working in parallel... Reviews are billed on token usage and generally average $15–25

claim: Devin Review, launched January 2026 by Cognition, reorganizes diffs to group logically connected changes with explanations and interactive chat, and was free during its early-access phase; Cognition closed a $1B+ Series D at a $26B valuation on May 27, 2026.
quote: The most direct competitor is Devin Review, launched in January 2026 by Cognition... Devin Review is free during its early access phase. Devin Review intelligently reorganizes diffs... On May 27, 2026, Cognition AI closed a Series D of more than $1 billion at a $26 billion valuation

claim: Both Gemini Code Assist and Amazon Q Developer cost $19/user/month (Standard); Gemini reviews PRs via the /gemini comment tag pulling repo context, while Amazon Q's GitHub integration (code review, issue-to-PR) remained in preview in 2026.
quote: Both Gemini Code Assist and Amazon Q Developer cost $19/user/month... Gemini Code Assist allows reviewing pull requests by adding the /gemini tag to comments... For Amazon Q Developer, GitHub integration remains in preview status

claim: Qodo Merge is the commercial product built on the open-source PR-Agent engine and is self-hostable free with your own LLM keys (Qodo 2.0 launched Feb 2026 with multi-agent bug/security/quality/test agents); Greptile self-hosts only on custom enterprise contracts, and CodeRabbit self-hosting is Enterprise-only with a 500-seat minimum at ~$15,000/month.
quote: Qodo Merge is the commercial product built on top of PR-Agent... can be self-hosted with your own LLM API keys for free. Qodo 2.0 launched in February 2026 with a multi-agent architecture... CodeRabbit only offers self-hosted deployment on its Enterprise plan with a 500-seat minimum at approximately $15,000/month

claim: Qodo's open-source PR-Agent (the engine under Qodo Merge, migrated from the Codium-ai namespace) is the original open-source PR reviewer for automated PR analysis, feedback and suggestions.
quote: PR Agent: The Original Open-Source PR Reviewer. This project It is not the Qodo free tier.

claim: Sourcery is an actively maintained MIT-licensed open-source code-quality/review tool (v1.43.0 released Jan 19 2026) with IDE integrations for PyCharm, VS Code, Sublime and Vim, free for public/open-source repos.
quote: Sourcery is completely free to use for public repos/open source projects

claim: Baz publishes baz-scm/awesome-reviewers, an open-source library of ready-to-use system prompts for agentic code review.
quote: Ready-to-use system prompts for Agentic Code Review.

claim: On SWR-Bench (1000 verified GitHub PRs across 12 Python projects), the best LLM code-review system (PR-Review + Gemini-2.5-Pro) reached only F1=19.38%, precision=16.65%, recall=23.18%; all techniques had precision below ~17%, indicating high false-positive rates.
quote: all techniques exhibited precision scores below 10%. This implies...developers would need to invest considerable additional effort

claim: Greptile's July 2025 vendor benchmark on 50 real-world bugs across 5 repos reported catch rates of Greptile 82%, Bugbot 58%, Copilot 54%, CodeRabbit 44%, Graphite 6%, counting a catch only when a tool gave an explicit line-level comment; no false-positive rate was published.
quote: A bug was counted as caught only when the tool provided an explicit line-level PR comment that points to the faulty code and explains the impact.

claim: METR's randomized controlled trial (16 experienced open-source devs, 246 tasks, early-2025 frontier tools/Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7) found AI tooling increased task completion time by 19%, despite developers forecasting a 24% speedup and estimating a 20% speedup afterward.
quote: When AI tools are allowed, developers take 19% longer to complete issues

claim: The DORA 2025 report shows AI raises individual throughput (+21% tasks, ~+98% PRs merged) but median PR review time rises (+91%), PR size grows (+154%), and quality signals worsen, with organizational delivery metrics staying flat.
quote: individual throughput increases but downstream quality and stability issues compound, creating organizational friction that offsets gains

claim: CodeRabbit's December 2025 study of 470 real-world open-source PRs found AI-authored changes carry up to 1.7x more critical/major defects, 75% more logic/correctness issues, 1.5-2x more security vulnerabilities, and ~8x more performance inefficiencies than human code (vendor report).
quote: Critical and major defects are up to 1.7x higher in AI-authored changes

claim: A 2026 survey of 99 code-review benchmark papers (58 pre-LLM, 41 LLM era, 2015-2025) finds datasets are scattered with inconsistent design and that progress is hindered by a lack of systematic, standardized evaluation, with limited dynamic/runtime evaluation.
quote: scattered, vary widely in design, and provide limited insight into what review capabilities are actually being assessed

claim: Prompt injection via a PR title hijacked Anthropic's Claude Code Security Review, Google's Gemini CLI Action, and GitHub's Copilot agent to leak API keys and tokens, yet vendors paid small bounties and published no CVEs.
quote: crafted a PR title containing a prompt injection payload. Claude executed the embedded commands... Anthropic: $100 bounty; severity rating upgraded from 9.3 to 9.4... None of the three vendors assigned CVEs or published advisories

claim: The 'Comment and Control' attack class writes a payload into a PR title, issue body, or comment; the agent treats it as trusted and exfiltrates credentials back through GitHub's own APIs, bypassing env-var filtering and secret scanning.
quote: a malicious payload is written into a GitHub pull request title, issue body, or comment, and when an AI coding agent processes that content, it treats the attacker's instructions as trusted and executes them — typically exfiltrating API keys and access tokens back through GitHub itself

claim: GitGuardian found 28.6M new secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025 (a 34% YoY jump), and commits co-authored by Claude Code leaked secrets at roughly double the baseline rate, showing agent-accelerated code outpaces credential governance.
quote: 28,649,024 new secrets exposed in public GitHub commits across 2025, a 34% year-over-year increase... Commits co-authored by Claude Code leaked secrets at roughly double the baseline rate... Integration velocity can increase by 10x, but credential governance doesn't scale at the same rate

claim: AI review systematically misses business logic, architecture, edge cases, and context-dependent security because it does not know what the application is supposed to do; false-positive alert fatigue erodes trust faster than missed issues.
quote: AI lacks understanding of your product's unique requirements... Design patterns, system boundaries, and long-term scalability implications require experience and context AI doesn't possess... Context-dependent security issues often slip through because AI doesn't know what your application is supposed to do... Alert fatigue...erodes trust faster than missed issues

claim: AI review fatigue leads developers to rubber-stamp suggestions and within a month skim or ignore comments entirely; performance degrades on PRs over 500 lines, and self-review bias arises when the same model writes and reviews code.
quote: developers start rubber-stamping AI suggestions without critical evaluation... After a month, they are skimming or ignoring AI comments entirely... performance deteriorates on changes exceeding 500 lines... when the same AI model generates code and reviews it, there's risk of self-review bias

claim: CodeRabbit reviews aggressively but at roughly 50.5% precision, meaning about half of its comments point to real issues and the other half are noise, cluttering PRs.
quote: 50.5% precision means roughly half of CodeRabbit's comments point to real issues. The other half are suggestions that may not be actionable... reviews aggressively... Produces more comments, some of which are noise

claim: Practitioners report AI introduces security headaches reviews miss: hardcoded secrets, credentials exposed in logs/workflows, unsafe curl|bash suggestions, and untraceable agent actions using shared API keys.
quote: Secrets leaking left and right — AI suggesting code that hardcodes stuff or exposes creds in logs/workflows... when an agent makes a call using a shared API key and something goes wrong, there is no way to prove what it was authorized to do... secrets passed as shell args, pasted into logs, broad credentials reused across runs

claim: CodeRabbit is configured via a .coderabbit.yaml supporting path_filters (glob include/exclude), path_instructions mapping globs to custom guidance, code_guidelines scanning convention files, learnings.scope (local/global/auto), and pre_merge_checks with off/warning/error enforcement levels.
quote: Pre-merge Checks (pre_merge_checks): Define enforcement levels per check—"off" (disabled), "warning" (notification only), or "error" (blocks merging if request-changes workflow enabled).

claim: A safer CI pattern grants the review agent only contents:read and pull-requests:write, generates patches as files that are never auto-applied, and uses trust-tier rollout where low-risk repos auto-publish validated comments while high-risk repos restrict the agent to draft summaries needing human approval.
quote: Trust-tier rollout: Repositories are classified by risk level, with low-risk repos allowing auto-published comments after validation, while high-risk repos restrict the agent to draft summaries requiring human approval.

claim: Cloudflare's production AI review uses a bias-toward-approval model: single warnings yield approved_with_comments, only critical/production-risk patterns trigger requested_changes blocks, with a break-glass override used in 0.6% of cases.
quote: Single warnings in otherwise clean code receive approved_with_comments rather than blocks. Only critical items or patterns suggesting production risk trigger merge blocks via requested_changes.

claim: Severity-based quality gates define thresholds per category (Critical/High/Medium/Low) for new vs overall code, exiting non-zero to block merges when critical issues exceed zero, and can run alongside SonarQube as independent required status checks.
quote: A simple custom implementation filters findings by severity and exits with a non-zero code when critical issues exceed zero or high-severity issues exceed a configured threshold, blocking the merge.

claim: Semgrep's auto-triage handles roughly 60% of incoming security triage automatically with Memories enabled while maintaining 96% agreement with security researchers on true positives, and a 'not a bug' feedback button routes false positives to teams for rule tuning since the noisiest five rules cause most false positives.
quote: Semgrep's auto-triage system handles approximately 60% of incoming security triage work automatically when Memories are enabled, while maintaining 96% agreement with security researchers on true positive identification.

claim: A typical AI code review costs $0.03-$0.06 (up to $0.10-$0.20 for large PRs or rich prompts), and model routing classifies request difficulty for ~$0.001/request, saving roughly 50% of model cost by sending simple tasks to cheaper models like Sonnet and reserving Opus for architectural decisions.
quote: Model routing classifies requests by difficulty and routes them to appropriate models at a cost of approximately $0.001 per request, saving roughly 50% of model costs if half of tasks are simple.

claim: Automated review evolved through three generations: deterministic linters/static analysis (ESLint, SonarQube, Semgrep), then LLM PR bots that summarize diffs and flag semantic issues (CodeRabbit, Qodo), then agentic reviewers framed as reasoning systems on top of a retrieval system.
quote: Automated code review used to mean a linter catching a missing semicolon... A code review agent is a reasoning system on top of a retrieval system. When the retrieval layer is 'the diff plus 100 lines around it,' every AI reviewer regresses to the same ceiling.

claim: Facebook's Getafix (2018) was an early industrially-deployed auto-fix tool that learned fix patterns from past human edits via hierarchical clustering and suggested fixes for bugs found by the Infer static analyzer, with engineers approving before deployment.
quote: learns from engineers' previous changes to the codebase. It finds hidden patterns... suggests fixes for bugs found by Infer, our static analysis tool that identifies issues such as null pointer exceptions

claim: By 2026 AI-generated code acceptance rose from 20% to 60% and PRs merged without any review (human or agentic) are up 31.3%, while bugs per developer rose to 54% and the incidents-to-PR ratio climbed 242.7% under high AI adoption, evidencing a review-capacity gap.
quote: The acceptance rate of AI-generated code has risen from 20% to 60%... Pull requests merged without any review, human or agentic, are up 31.3%... The incidents-to-PR ratio is up 242.7% as teams move from low to high AI adoption

claim: As of early 2026 roughly 41% of all code is AI-generated and the volume is projected to outstrip human review capacity by 40%, the 'AI code generation gap' driving demand for automated review.
quote: by 2026, the volume of AI-generated code is projected to outstrip human review capacity by 40%, creating what experts call the 'AI code generation gap'

claim: 2025-26 agentic review tools handle the full PR lifecycle: agents get their own git worktree, branch and PR, autonomously fix CI failures and address reviewer comments, returning a structured result with a follow-up action like creating a fix PR or commit.
quote: Each agent gets its own git worktree, its own branch, and its own PR. When CI fails, the agent fixes it. When reviewers leave comments, the agent addresses them.

claim: The 'why now' for agentic review hinges on MCP, introduced by Anthropic in 2024 as an open standard for connecting agents to tools/data; by 2026 it became table stakes with 97M+ monthly downloads, fixing the brittle tool-integration layer that had bottlenecked capable models.
quote: The Model Context Protocol was introduced in 2024 by Anthropic as an open-source standard... while models had become more capable, the way agents interacted with external systems remained fragmented and brittle... 97M+ monthly downloads

claim: The forward look centers on verifier agents because human reviewers are rubber-stamping AI PRs from fatigue; tools like CodeRabbit's Autofix spawn their own coding agent to write a fix and commit it, while human oversight remains mandatory for architectural alignment.
quote: human reviewers are rubber-stamping AI-generated pull requests out of sheer fatigue... CodeRabbit's Autofix spawns its own coding agent to write the fix and commit to the branch

claim: Production agentic review tools now pre-review every PR with AI agents, presenting human reviewers with a prioritized list of issues, suggested fixes, and ready-to-merge changes to reduce backlog.
quote: Qodo reduces PR backlog by pre-reviewing every pull request with AI agents, so human reviewers start with a prioritized list of issues, suggested fixes, and ready-to-merge changes
